messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajesh is a 58-year-old widowed fisherman who lives alone in a small coastal town. Three years ago, while hauling in his nets before dawn, a sudden squall capsized his boat. He was trapped in the dark water, his chest crushed against the hull as the vessel rolled, and he inhaled seawater before being thrown clear. He treaded water for nearly an hour, certain he would drown, before a passing trawler found him. He remembers that the silence after the boat went under—the absence of the engine, the wind, even his own shouts—was the most terrifying thing he had ever experienced.

In the months that followed, Rajesh tried to return to work, but the moment he stepped onto the dock, the memory would surge back with the same raw terror he had felt in the water. He would be standing there, and suddenly he could not find the words to describe what had happened; the event felt present, not past, as if he were still pinned beneath the boat. The crash of waves against a pier, or the sight of a car that had been in an accident on the coastal road, could instantly trigger this feeling, and he would freeze, his mouth dry and his heart hammering.

Rajesh began to feel that he could no longer trust his own body. His legs would shake for no reason, his lungs would seize up, and he came to believe that his physical self had betrayed him. This sense of bodily unreliability bled into a deeper loss: he felt he did not know himself anymore. The man who had navigated storms and mended nets for thirty years was gone, replaced by someone who jumped at the creak of a floorboard. He also grew convinced that people were not what they seemed. When a stranger on the street asked him for directions, Rajesh would hear a hidden threat in their voice, and he would mutter an excuse and walk away, certain they meant him harm.

This distrust kept him alert even inside his own home. He would sit in his kitchen, rigid, listening to the unusual silence of the house, convinced that something dangerous was about to happen. He constantly scanned his surroundings for signs of danger, and every unexpected sound—a gull landing on the roof, a neighbor’s door closing—would send his mind back to that moment of silence before the capsize. The threat he felt in his own living room would then trigger the memory again, and he would be back in the water, gasping.

Over time, the cycle tightened. The more he distrusted others and his own body, the more hypervigilant he became, and the more he scanned for danger, the more likely he was to encounter a trigger—a stranger’s glance, a mention of someone losing a loved one in a storm. Each trigger then reinforced his negative appraisals: he was not the man he used to be, and the world was full of hidden threats. He stopped going to the harbor entirely, telling himself he was being sensible, but the isolation only deepened his sense of identity loss.

What finally brought Rajesh to seek help was a moment on his porch last month. A neighbor stopped by to talk about his wife’s recent death, and Rajesh felt the memory of his own wife—lost to illness years before the accident—crash into the terror of the drowning. He could not breathe, could not speak, and he realized he had not left his house in two weeks. He is most afraid that he will never feel safe again, but he is also quietly hoping that someone can help him find the words he has lost.
